title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
authors: Xuwei Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Xiaoguang Hu, Zhongwei Liu, Yuanhui Sun, Jun Huo
abstract: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

infographic.key_insight: PaddleMaterials unifies six materials-learning task classes in one toolkit while preserving task-specific representations and physical semantics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can compose materials workflows and enable compiled execution with one setting, without changing model definitions.
method: Standardize data processing, training, evaluation and pretrained-model management.
Record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references for verifiable cross-task composition.

infographic.watch_item: The reported case studies do not establish generalization across materials chemistries, and compiled acceleration was not universal across all model groups.
infographic.paper_title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science

title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
authors: Makoto Takamoto, Chaitanya Sampara, Viktor Zaverkin, Daniel Oñoro-Rubio, Mathias Niepert
abstract: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

infographic.key_insight: Geometry-based fragmentation creates tunable, multiscale molecular representations without predefined chemical fragmentation rules for polymer property prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining polymer sequence representations with 3D fragment information can improve prediction of several properties relevant to materials screening.
method: Formulate fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization inspired by k-center, with fragment count determined by the radius.
Vary the radius to construct multiscale fragments using largely geometric information.
Integrate geometric fragment attention into a multimodal model combining p-SMILES and 3D conformations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset report improved accuracy for several properties over p-SMILES-only models, with explainability analyses probing physical relevance.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify gains or establish how robust predictions are to conformer choice and fragmentation radius.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction

title: SteelAgent: LLM-Orchestrated, Physics-Informed Steel Property Prediction with Audited Generalization and Calibrated Uncertainty
authors: Aleksandr Volkov, Roman Sultimov, Mikhail Kuzin, Yury Maximov
abstract: Steel property models can perform well on random test splits even when they extrapolate poorly to unfamiliar alloys. SteelAgent couples metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with a language-model interface for property prediction, uncertainty reporting and inverse design. We examine how the choice of held-out unit changes the conclusions drawn from SteelBench tensile-strength evaluations. For gradient boosting, pooled out-of-fold $R^2$ fell from 0.859 on a random split to 0.113 when steel families were held out. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals ranged from 91.0% under random splitting to 37.6% on held-out sources. The effect of physics-derived features depended on the evaluation. They increased gradient-boosting $R^2$ by 0.2534 in a 17-family holdout analysis and decreased it by 0.358 in a separate four-grade laboratory analysis. We report group-level errors and a synthetic regression experiment illustrating how calibration can deteriorate on held-out groups. These results motivate reporting the evaluation population alongside a property estimate or compliance score.

infographic.key_insight: SteelAgent’s apparent prediction accuracy and uncertainty reliability drop sharply when evaluation holds out unfamiliar steel families or data sources.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Steel property estimates and compliance scores should identify the evaluation population before informing alloy selection or inverse design.
method: Combine metallurgical descriptors and machine-learning models with an LLM interface.
Audit generalization using random, steel-family and source-held-out evaluations.
Assess prediction-interval coverage, physics-feature effects and group-level errors.

title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
authors: YuJie Liu, Dezhen Xue, Jun Sun, Xiangdong Ding, Zhibin Gao, Turab Lookman
abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

infographic.key_insight: General-purpose LLMs outperformed domain-specific pretrained models for alloy property prediction, with further gains from numerical estimates supplied by prior models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining general-purpose LLMs with existing predictors and carefully selected reference data could reduce the cost of alloy property screening.
method: Benchmark general-purpose LLMs against SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT across Ti, steels, high-entropy alloys, and Al.
Prompt DeepSeek V3.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash with CatBoost or SteelBERT estimates to guide prediction correction.
Evaluate reference-data similarity and self-reported confidence alongside prediction accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that using only 5% of high-similarity training references achieved performance similar to using the full training set, while high self-reported confidence correlated with smaller errors.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical error metrics or detailed out-of-distribution results, so robustness on unfamiliar alloy compositions remains to be verified.
infographic.paper_title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction

title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations
authors: Jiacheng Cen, Anyi Li, Ning Lin, Zihe Wang, Ji-Rong Wen, Wenbing Huang
abstract: Symmetry governs the organization of physical structures, while symmetry breaking reveals their transformations. In geometric deep learning, symmetry imposes rank constraints on equivariant representations, limiting the expressive capacity of equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs). Here we show that these constraints can instead be exploited: the singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide a unified fingerprint of structural symmetry. We introduce spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which enable discrete point-group identification through rank-template matching and continuous symmetry analysis by quantifying spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enabling a parameter-free GNN implementation. Its spectra can be reused across multiple target groups, and the resulting leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, SymFP accurately identifies point groups, tracks controlled symmetry breaking and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that can be obscured by global geometric measures. These results establish the spectral structure of equivariant representations as a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems.

infographic.key_insight: Singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide orientation-invariant fingerprints for identifying structural symmetry and tracking symmetry breaking.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SymFP offers a reusable symmetry diagnostic for crystals, molecules and complex assemblies, including local changes that global geometric measures can obscure.
method: Extract singular-value spectra from equivariant representations using an architecture-agnostic framework.
Identify discrete point groups by matching spectra to symmetry-imposed rank templates.
Quantify continuous symmetry breaking through spectral energy beyond target rank constraints, with subgroup-monotonic leakage scores.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate point-group identification and controlled symmetry-breaking tracking across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, without numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Practical robustness to noisy coordinates and numerical rank thresholds is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations

title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation
authors: Shoeb Athar, Jérémy Guazzagaloppa, Philippe Jund
abstract: Resorcinol-formaldehyde (RF) aerogels are lightweight, ultra-porous thermal superinsulators whose complex amorphous structure has not yet been described at the all-atom level. Here, we build an all-atom model of the RF aerogel skeleton by combining density functional theory (DFT) and classical molecular dynamics (MD), validate it against experimental infrared and density measurements, and use it to study the incorporation of iron dopants. The RF base unit was optimized with Gaussian, DMol$^{3}$ and SIESTA, and its calculated infrared spectrum agreed with experiment. Comparing classical force fields with DFT for branched systems of two to four base units (140-278 atoms) led to the choice of COMPASS II. A 15,012-atom system of 54 branched RF units, not cross-linked to each other, aggregated into a single cluster in the canonical (NVT) ensemble and reached an equilibrium density of 1.296 g.cm$^{-3}$ in the isobaric-isothermal (NPT) ensemble, in agreement with the experimental skeletal density (1.3 g.cm$^{-3}$). Then, 5 wt$\%$ iron (109 atoms) was added to the equilibrated structure: during 1 ns of NPT simulation, the fraction of iron atoms embedded in the skeleton rose from 63$\%$ to 71$\%$, and the Fe-C radial distribution function peaked at 3 Å. The model thus provides an experimentally supported starting point for screening fillers and dopants in RF gels, with prospective application to their thermoelectric functionalization, which we have previously demonstrated experimentally with basalt and PANOX fibres. Future extensions could address skeleton properties relevant to thermal insulation and the pyrolysis of RF gels into carbon and metal-doped carbon aerogels.

infographic.key_insight: A DFT-guided all-atom model reproduces key experimental features of the resorcinol-formaldehyde aerogel skeleton and enables atomistic study of iron incorporation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model provides a starting point for screening fillers and dopants for RF aerogels, with potential applications in thermoelectric functionalization and thermal insulation.
method: Optimize RF base units with DFT and compare calculated infrared spectra with experiment.
Benchmark force fields against DFT for branched RF units and select COMPASS II.
Simulate skeleton aggregation and density equilibration, then track 5 wt% iron incorporation over 1 ns.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 15,012-atom model reached 1.296 g/cm³ versus an experimental skeletal density of 1.3 g/cm³; after iron addition, the embedded fraction rose from 63% to 71%.
infographic.watch_item: The branched RF units were not cross-linked to one another, and agreement with infrared spectra and skeletal density does not establish bulk thermal or thermoelectric performance.
infographic.paper_title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation

title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
authors: Junchi Liu, Haoran Si, Luo Yan, Sergei Tretiak, Liujiang Zhou
abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: ST2M uses crystal symmetry to guide generation, achieving 96.37% structural validity while improving the yield of stable, unique, and novel candidates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Generating candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints could accelerate materials screening and reduce wasted downstream calculations.
method: Represent crystals as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits.
Condition discrete–continuous diffusion on Wyckoff patterns and apply degree-of-freedom masks.
Use a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables.

infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify performance on unknown Wyckoff patterns, and first-principles validation covers only selected candidates.
infographic.paper_title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation

title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations
authors: Hrishi V. Harsora, Ashutosh Krishna Amaram, Raghavan Ranganathan, Tarun K. Agarwal
abstract: Conventional process optimization of the Metal-Organic Chemical Vapor Deposition (MOCVD) growth parameters to achieve high-quality thin films relies on iterative, resource-intensive experimental runs. While predictive modeling can circumvent this cost and effort, simulating thin-film growth is constrained by the vastly different length and time scales of the deposition process. While continuum (e.g., Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)) and first-principles methods (e.g., Molecular Dynamics (MD)) struggle to balance experimental length/time scales and atomistic accuracy, Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) bridges this divide by resolving atomistic events whilst remaining tractable at experimental length and time scales. However, the accuracy of KMC relies on kinetic rate parameters that require costly density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In order to circumvent this, we present a framework that calibrates the rate parameters directly against experimental growth data. A forward KMC growth model is coupled in a closed loop with a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) optimizer that navigates the high-dimensional parameter space, with the search steered by the degree of rate control of each reaction rate parameter. The approach invokes no material-specific assumptions and hence, any deposition process whose forward kinetics can be reduced to a set of rate-controlled events is amenable to the same treatment. We demonstrate it for the MOCVD of GaAs, where the calibrated model captures the characteristic temperature dependence of the measured growth rate. The framework is also able to recover the three well known kinetic regimes characterized by change in the rate determining step from precursor chemisorption to desorption. As a result, the framework converts routinely measured growth data into a mechanistically interpretable model of the deposition process.

infographic.key_insight: A closed-loop optimizer calibrates atomistic GaAs growth kinetics directly from experimental growth data, reducing reliance on costly DFT-derived rate parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework turns routinely measured MOCVD growth rates into mechanistic insight that could support less experiment-intensive process optimization.
method: Simulate deposition through atomistic, rate-controlled events using kinetic Monte Carlo.
Calibrate kinetic parameters against experimental growth data using Monte Carlo Tree Search.
Steer the search using each reaction parameter’s degree of rate control.
infographic.evidence_signal: For GaAs MOCVD, the calibrated model captures the measured growth rate’s temperature dependence and recovers three known kinetic regimes with changing rate-determining steps.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify predictive errors or establish generalization beyond the GaAs calibration case.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic Insights into MOCVD Growth of GaAs using a Closed Loop Autonomous System Combining Directed Reinforcement Learning and Kinetic Monte Carlo Simulations

title: PolyGPT: A Decoder-Only Transformer for Polymer Electrolyte Design
authors: Tanmay Sarkar Akash, Siddhartha Das
abstract: Designing polymer electrolytes requires control over both material properties and chemical structure. Here, we present PolyGPT, a Transformer with 38.3 million parameters that generates polymer repeat units from optional property targets, requests to include or exclude a specified chemical feature, and an electrolyte-domain condition. Using the model selected by validation loss, we compared unconditional generation with requests for electrolyte-associated structures, a low glass-transition temperature (Tg), or both. Unconditional and electrolyte-only generation achieved structural validity of 99.46% and 99.59%, respectively. However, electrolyte conditioning increased repetition: uniqueness among valid outputs fell from 99.99% to 51.74%. At a Tg target of 246.11 K, we compared generation with and without electrolyte conditioning, and adding the electrolyte condition slightly reduced the predictor-estimated mean absolute error from 26.97 to 26.07 K, but the fraction of all attempts yielding distinct valid polymers within 50 K of the target fell from 82.35% to 32.31%. When we also required absence from the training catalog, these yields were 59.90% and 19.71%, respectively. The lower yield persisted with a tighter 25 K tolerance. Domain conditioning also weakened control of inclusion requests: the mean fraction of attempts producing valid polymers containing the requested chemical feature fell from 94.27% to 31.27%. Across nine checkpoints, earlier models sometimes produced more distinct, catalog-unseen polymers meeting the Tg target: 10,000 checkpoint model with electrolyte conditioning and 30,000 checkpoint model without it. Together, these results show why property error alone is insufficient for evaluating conditional polymer generation. It must be considered alongside repetition, training-catalog novelty, and whether combined design requests are satisfied.

infographic.key_insight: Electrolyte conditioning preserves high structural validity but increases repetition and reduces distinct polymers satisfying combined design requests, despite slightly improving predicted property error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Polymer design workflows should evaluate distinct usable candidates and chemical constraints alongside property accuracy.
method: A 38.3-million-parameter decoder-only Transformer generates polymer repeat units.
Optional controls specify property targets, chemical-feature inclusion or exclusion, and electrolyte-domain conditioning.

infographic.paper_title: PolyGPT: A Decoder-Only Transformer for Polymer Electrolyte Design

title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
authors: Eliane Younes, Elie Hachem, Marc Bernacki
abstract: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning a recurrent forecasting model on temperature and thermal rate enables accurate prediction of grain size distributions during non-isothermal heat treatment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce reliance on costly grain-growth simulations when evaluating heat-treatment schedules for polycrystalline materials.
method: Encode grain size distributions with a convolutional neural network.
Embed instantaneous temperature and thermal rate with a dedicated multilayer perceptron.
Forecast microstructural evolution with a recurrent network trained on validated front-tracking simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: K-fold cross-validation yielded mean relative errors of 2.99% for one-hour cycles and 4.51% for four-hour cycles, with R² above 0.99; ten simulations spanning four unseen thermal histories yielded errors of 1.91–14.66%.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation is simulation-based, and errors reaching 14.66% on unseen thermal histories warrant caution when applying the model beyond its training conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials

title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery
authors: Aditya Raghavan, Sergei V Kalinin
abstract: Structure property prediction is a classical task in machine learning, ranging from molecular activity and materials properties to local functional responses measured in microscopy. For image-based regression, two choices define the information available to the predictor: the size of the image neighborhood and the spatial resolution retained within it. A small neighborhood can omit relevant surrounding structure, whereas a large, finely sampled neighborhood can introduce redundant or irrelevant information. Here, we develop a framework for constructing spatial descriptors for prediction of local spectra and hysteresis loops. We benchmark regression models, use SHAP maps to examine their spatial attribution, and explore the effect of the patch size and compression to establish the relationship between predictive accuracy and descriptor dimensionality. We then use a genetic algorithm to optimize spatial partitions and the assignment of mean, minimum, and maximum pooling operations. Each retained region contributes an explicit measurement of the image, allowing the search to balance prediction error against the number of descriptor values. Cartesian and polar constructions provide complementary ways to organize this information. The resulting descriptors make it possible to examine where spatial detail is needed, where regional summaries are sufficient, and how these choices depend on the predictor and the measured response. The same approach can be used for molecules and solids once the genetic algorithm rules for these are established.

infographic.key_insight: Genetic algorithms design interpretable spatial descriptors that balance local-response prediction error against the number of image-derived features.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact, explicit image measurements can help engineers identify which surrounding structures matter for predicting local spectra and hysteresis loops.
method: Benchmark regression models and use SHAP maps to examine spatial attribution.
Evaluate how image patch size and compression affect accuracy and descriptor dimensionality.
Evolve Cartesian and polar partitions with mean, minimum, and maximum pooling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes regression benchmarking and accuracy–dimensionality evaluation for local spectra and hysteresis loops, but reports no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Extension to molecules and solids requires new genetic algorithm rules and is not demonstrated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery

title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications
authors: MD Tanzib Ehsan Sanglap, Ans Al Rashid, Abdullah Sayam, Injamamul Arief, Andrei G. Shvarts, Lukasz Kaczmarczyk
abstract: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency mechanical energy into electricity and enable self-powered sensing. Their performance depends on interactions among material properties, surface morphology, contact mechanics, charge generation and external circuits. This review examines these interactions across length scales to assess how material and interface descriptions support predictive device design. Polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials are discussed in relation to charge generation and retention, mechanical compliance, durability and application requirements. Modelling approaches span molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations, rough-surface contact mechanics, device-scale electrostatics and equivalent circuits. Their capabilities are assessed through the inputs they require, the quantities they predict and the experimental evidence used for validation. Particular attention is given to prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions, which constrain predictions under realistic loading conditions. Applications are organised by macroscale, milliscale and microscale device dimensions to examine requirements for materials, architecture and integration. The review identifies evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay as critical links between interfacial behaviour and electrical output. A staged validation strategy is proposed for contact mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response, with independent testing beyond calibration conditions. These priorities guide the development of multiscale models and reliable TENG systems.

infographic.key_insight: Predictive triboelectric nanogenerator design requires linking evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay to electrical output across length scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupling materials, interface mechanics and circuit behaviour can guide more reliable energy harvesters and self-powered sensors.
method: Reviews polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials against charge retention, compliance and durability requirements.
Assesses modelling from atomistic calculations and rough-surface contact mechanics to device electrostatics and equivalent circuits.
Organises applications by device scale and proposes staged validation of mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review assesses model inputs, predicted quantities and experimental validation evidence, while advocating independent testing beyond calibration conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Prescribed surface charge, idealised geometry and nominal contact-area assumptions can limit predictions under realistic loading.
infographic.paper_title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications

title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials
authors: Denisse Córdova Carrizales, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, L. Dagny Davis, Jeremy Ramsey, Ryotaro Okabe, Mouyang Cheng
abstract: Spatially programmed functional materials, from functionally graded alloys and metamaterials to quantum superlattices, use their spatial structure to tailor physical properties. However, translating a desired spatial structure into a practical fabrication recipe remains challenging due to the complex relationship between processing conditions and resulting material structures. Here we show that a large language model (LLM) agent can inverse-design such fabrication recipes by using a physics-based simulator of ion-matter interactions as a tool. Given an arbitrary depth profile of implanted ions or vacancies, the agent selects the ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers; writes, runs, and interprets simulations; and iteratively refines the recipe until the simulated profile matches the target, with minimal human input. Our work demonstrates physics-guided agentic inverse design as a practical approach to making the spatial structure of materials a programmable variable, opening new opportunities to explore emergent physical phenomena and functional phases of matter.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM agent uses physics simulations to inverse-design fabrication recipes for target depth profiles of implanted ions or vacancies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help engineers translate desired spatial material structures into ion-processing recipes with minimal human input.
method: Specify a target ion or vacancy depth profile.
Have the agent select ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers.
Run and interpret ion–matter simulations, iteratively refining the recipe to match the target.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulated matching of target depth profiles but provides no quantitative accuracy metrics, benchmark comparisons, or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical fabrication accuracy remains dependent on simulator fidelity and experimental verification.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials

title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
authors: Shi Yin, Zujian Dai, Xinyang Pan, Lixin He
abstract: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

infographic.key_insight: DP-Learner predicts electronic-structure Hamiltonians directly as orbital-and-spin operator blocks, avoiding the representation mismatch of conventional irreducible-tensor features.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Preserving Hamiltonian block structure offers a route to more accurate predictions and more efficient computation for materials modeling.
method: Perform Transformer message passing directly in Hamiltonian-like direct-product space.
Use Lie-generator directional embeddings and equivariant left–right products and contractions without explicit Clebsch–Gordan decomposition.
Route interactions through invariant scalar gating, attention, and environment-dependent context.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors introduce MP-HAM-110K with over 110,000 structures spanning 68 elements and Hamiltonian/wavefunction data, and report improved accuracy and inference efficiency on it and Materials-HAM-SOC.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical gains or hardware details, so practical speedups and memory costs require checking the full benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction

title: Complex Martensitic Microstructures in ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$
authors: John M. Ball, Francesco Della Porta, Tomonari Inamura
abstract: We analyze the unusual microstructure resulting from the cubic to orthorhombic phase transformation in the shape-memory alloy ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$. This seems to represent an approximate experimental realization of a deformation having a finite number of incompatible deformation gradients, which has been known to exist only as a theoretical possibility. Because the middle eigenvalue $γ$ of the transformation strain is very close to 1, the phase transformation in this alloy takes place via nucleation of exact austenite-martensite interfaces rather than, as usual for other alloys, by classical austenite-martensite interfaces separating the austenite from a finely-twinned laminate of martensite. According to the moving mask approximation of Della Porta this leads to the question whether a microstructure can be formed from the set $H$ of the twelve matrices ${\mathbf V}_i$ on the martensite energy wells that are rank-one connected to the identity, even though these matrices are mutually incompatible. We show that when $γ=1$ and the transformation is volume preserving, such a microstructure is possible that does not deform the grain boundary. This is a consequence of $H$ forming a degenerate $T_{12}$ configuration in the sense of Kirchheim. In fact there are such microstructures supported on just 8 of the 12 matrices in $H$. However there is no deformation satisfying the same boundary condition whose gradient belongs to $H$ almost everywhere. An additional prediction, confirmed experimentally, is that the macroscopic deformation gradient equals the identity everywhere. We also analyse the approximate compatibility of the ${\mathbf V}_i$. Although mutually incompatible, they are nearly compatible, with some pairs much more nearly compatible than others, these pairs corresponding to interfaces that are more frequently observed.

infographic.key_insight: Mutually incompatible martensitic variants in Ti₇₆Nb₂₂Al₂ can support a fine-scale microstructure with no macroscopic deformation through a degenerate T₁₂ configuration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis helps explain how shape-memory alloys can transform without deforming grain boundaries and why certain variant interfaces occur more frequently.
method: Apply the moving-mask approximation to 12 martensitic gradients rank-one connected to austenite.
Establish a degenerate T₁₂ configuration under unit middle eigenvalue and volume preservation, with microstructures supported on just 8 gradients.
Analyze pairwise near-compatibility to interpret observed interface frequencies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental confirmation of an identity macroscopic deformation gradient and associates more nearly compatible variant pairs with more frequently observed interfaces.
infographic.watch_item: The exact construction assumes unit middle eigenvalue and volume preservation; no deformation with the same boundary condition has its gradient in the finite variant set almost everywhere.
infographic.paper_title: Complex Martensitic Microstructures in ${\rm Ti}_{76}{\rm Nb}_{22}{\rm Al}_{2}$

title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model
authors: Jack Yang, Lei Ao, Sean Li
abstract: The rapid growth of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIP), particularly the foundational models for materials chemistry, such as MACE, has significantly strengthened our capabilities in studying the complex dynamics of materials through statistical sampling. Here, by performing molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE model, that are further combined with essential dynamics analysis, a tool that is commonly applied in (bio)molecular simulations, we examine the temperature-dependent ion dynamics in a prototypical inorganic solid superionic conductor, namely argyrodite Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl. Our analyses show clear localised phonon-like dynamics for Li$^+$ ions below 500 K with trajectories lying in a low-dimensional manifold that is highly nonlinear, which is opposite to the case in the high-temperature ($\sim$800 K) end. Between 500-700 K, the system exhibit strong competition in the dynamics between the Li$^+$ and framework ions, that are reflected in both the eigenspectrum and the projected low-dimensional embeddings characterising these dynamics not showing a simple monotonic dependency upon rising temperatures, and is further supported by investigations employing Langevin dynamics that systematically examine how damping the framework motions affects the dynamics of the Li$^+$ ions, thanks to the computational efficiency provided by MLIP. This work thus contributes towards the broader theoretical and data-driven framework for studying the lattice dynamics of solids.

infographic.key_insight: Fine-tuned MACE simulations reveal a shift from localized, nonlinear Li⁺ dynamics below 500 K to contrasting behavior near 800 K, with strong competition between Li⁺ and framework dynamics at 500–700 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding temperature-dependent coupling between mobile ions and the lattice can inform solid-electrolyte design and modeling.
method: Run molecular dynamics with a fine-tuned MACE interatomic potential.
Apply essential dynamics analysis to eigenspectra and low-dimensional trajectory embeddings.
Use Langevin dynamics to test how damping framework motion affects Li⁺ dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eigenspectra and trajectory embeddings show nonmonotonic temperature dependence at 500–700 K, supported by framework-damping simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report quantitative potential-validation errors or conductivity benchmarks, limiting assessment of predictive accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Temperature-Dependent Ion Dynamics in Argyrodite Superionic Conductor Li$_{6}$PS$_{5}$Cl with Fine-Tuned MACE Foundation Model

title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys
authors: Eric A. Lass, Carla Joyce C. Nocheseda, Christopher Tandoc, Yong-Jie Hu, Peter K. Liaw
abstract: Refractory compositionally complex alloys (R-CCAs) show great promise as next generation structural materials for extreme conditions, but alloys with excellent high temperature mechanical properties most often exhibit virtually zero room temperature tensile ductility, hindering potential commercial application. Several semi-empirical metrics have been employed for predicting plasticity in R-CCAs, including valence electron concentration, Pugh ratio, Rice criteria, and the D-parameter. While many currently available ductility metrics correlate very well when compressive plasticity is considered, only the density functional theory (DFT) based D-parameter shows a strong correlation in tension. A new ductility metric is developed using CALculation of PHAse Diagrams (CALPHAD) thermodynamics, Gamma, with includes the free energy difference between the body-centered cubic (BCC) and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phases, the interfacial free energy of a (110) BCC surface, and an electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion. The Gamma parameter exhibits better correlation with tensile ductility than D-parameter and performs equally well in compression. While this improvement is modest, a thermodynamically grounded ductility metric is clearly required to capture intrinsic ductility behavior. Extrinsic contributions to brittle behavior in R-CCAs, namely interstitial oxygen content, are also briefly discussed. Combining the Gamma ductility parameter with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility is proposed as a first order attempt to capture both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions to ductile behavior in R-CCAs.

infographic.key_insight: A new CALPHAD-based Γ ductility metric better correlates with tensile ductility in refractory compositionally complex alloys than the DFT-based D-parameter, while performing equally well in compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The metric could guide selection of refractory alloys that combine high-temperature performance with room-temperature tensile ductility.
method: Combine the BCC–HCP free-energy difference, (110) BCC surface interfacial free energy, and electronegativity-corrected lattice distortion.
Compare Γ with established ductility metrics for tensile and compressive plasticity.
Propose combining Γ with CALPHAD-calculated oxygen solubility to capture intrinsic and extrinsic ductility contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a modest improvement in tensile-ductility correlation over the D-parameter and comparable compression performance, without numerical evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed oxygen-solubility extension is a first-order approach, not an established predictor of oxygen-induced embrittlement.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamic Underpinnings Affecting Compressive and Tensile Plasticity in Refractory Compositionally Complex Alloys

title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
authors: S. -Y. Tseng
abstract: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $χ$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2χdz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.

infographic.key_insight: Seemingly different short mode-evolution coupler designs share one two-mode design space, with equivalent counter-diabatic realizations offering the same bandwidth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A lithography-aware rule broadens high-efficiency optical transfer by narrowing waveguide spacing at the anticrossing and using exact counter-diabatic control to suppress residual nonadiabatic coupling.
method: Unify width, spacing, and axis-bending designs using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers–Henneberger frame.
Relate bandwidth to the integrated light–steering-field misalignment on the Bloch sphere.
Evaluate designs with polymer-platform BPM simulations, particle swarm optimization, and three-dimensional BCB waveguide BPM.
infographic.evidence_signal: BPM simulations predict >99% transfer across 274 nm for a 500 µm coupler with a 1.05 µm minimum edge gap, versus 150 nm for a fixed-spacing-reference CD design at nearly the same gap; numerical optimization did not outperform the design rule.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is simulation-based; fabricated-device bandwidth and sensitivity to manufacturing tolerances remain to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers

title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
authors: Md Mahmudul Hasan Pathik
abstract: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

infographic.key_insight: Explicitly encoding chloride salt preparation enabled interpretable machine-learning predictions of molten-chloride corrosion, with the Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) emerging as the dominant descriptor.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support corrosion screening across alloys, salts, and exposure conditions while providing uncertainty estimates alongside predicted corrosion rates.
method: Compile 291 published static molten-chloride corrosion experiments.
Encode salt treatment, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurities using a graded CSPI.
Fit a blended tree ensemble; interpret predictions with sensitivity and SHAP analyses and quantify uncertainty with conformal intervals.
infographic.evidence_signal: The ensemble achieved cross-validated R² = 0.85 and MAE = 0.41 mg cm⁻² day⁻¹; conformal prediction intervals were reported as well calibrated.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence comes from heterogeneous static tests, so applicability to flowing salts or conditions beyond the compiled data requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network with exact boundary and initial constraints identifies the shear piezoelectric coefficient e15 from sparse, noisy simulated wavefields with low error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could enable non-destructive characterization of shear coupling for PMUT and surface acoustic wave devices, reducing reliance on destructive resonance tests.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers into network outputs to enforce boundary and initial conditions exactly.
Train on coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and sparse observations without boundary or initial-condition penalty weights.
Non-dimensionalize governing coefficients to improve numerical conditioning.
infographic.evidence_signal: On finite-element data from one subsurface line, the full formulation achieved 1.19% mean e15 error at 30 dB noise and 0.65–2.71% across a 40–0 dB sweep; displacement-only training also recovered e15.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-based; performance on experimental measurements and sensitivity to model or boundary-condition mismatch remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
